title: Classical Nahuatl — a demo language family

languages.name: Classical Nahuatl
languages.notes: The root of this demo family: Classical Nahuatl as recorded in 16th-century colonial sources for the Aztec capital and its hinterland. All 221 headwords are converted from the Wiktionary Classical Nahuatl lemmas; long vowels are marked with length, ⟨h⟩ is the glottal stop, and ⟨tz, ch, tl, ll, hu, qu⟩ map to their standard IPA values. There are no historical sound changes — synchronic allophony only.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

languages.name: Proto-Balto-Slavic Nahuatl
languages.notes: Proto-Balto-Slavic-style branch of the demo: labiovelar *kʷ simplifies to k, Winter-type lengthening applies before the Nahuatl glottal stop, the RUKI rule turns s into š after [k i], short o merges into a, the glottal stop is lost, and the Nahuatl lateral affricate and geminate lateral resolve to l. The first palatalization is a Slavic development and is not applied here. The old ā/ō token swap has been removed.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: The labiovelar loses its lip-rounding and merges with plain k, as in the Proto-Balto-Slavic simplification of *kʷ.
RUKI law narrowed to the historical triggers [k i] for this lexicon. The broader [l w j] trigger set was a demo artifact.
Winter-type lengthening of a before the Nahuatl glottal stop, a stand-in for the historical following plain voiced stop.
Winter-type lengthening of e before the Nahuatl glottal stop, a stand-in for the historical following plain voiced stop.
Winter-type lengthening of i before the Nahuatl glottal stop, a stand-in for the historical following plain voiced stop.
Winter-type lengthening of o before the Nahuatl glottal stop, a stand-in for the historical following plain voiced stop.
Short o merges into a, the regular Proto-Balto-Slavic merger. As a sequential child of Winter's law, it applies after o has lengthened before the glottal stop.
The glottal stop is lost after Winter-type lengthening, a simplified reflex of laryngeal loss.
The Nahuatl lateral affricate resolves to l; this is the single cleanup point for t͡ɬ in the Balto-Slavic branch.
The geminate lateral degeminates to l; this is the single cleanup point for lː in the Balto-Slavic branch.

languages.name: Baltic Nahuatl
languages.notes: Baltic-style daughter of Proto-Balto-Slavic: w hardens to v, long ē and ō diphthongize to ie and uo, intervocalic s and š voice to z and ž, and t͡s/t͡ʃ are preserved. The Nahuatl lateral affricate and geminate lateral were already resolved at Proto-Balto-Slavic.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: w hardens to v, a shared Baltic development.
PBS *ē diphthongizes to ie, the characteristic Baltic reflex.
PBS *ō diphthongizes to uo, the characteristic Baltic reflex.
Intervocalic s voices to z, supplying the voiced sibilant of the Baltic system.
Intervocalic š voices to ž, the voiced counterpart of š.

languages.name: Lithuanian Nahuatl
languages.notes: Lithuanian-style daughter of Baltic: Baltic *ā backs and rounds to o, n palatalizes to ɲ before front vowels (an adapted simplification), and the Baltic diphthongs ie/uo are inherited. Lithuanian preserves c [t͡s], č [t͡ʃ], z, and ž; the old č > š and s > š mergers have been removed.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: PBS *ā backs and rounds to o; Latvian, by contrast, preserves ā.
n palatalizes to ɲ before front vowels, an adapted simplification of Lithuanian palatalized n.

languages.name: Latvian Nahuatl
languages.notes: Latvian-style daughter of Baltic: ā and č are preserved, the inherited ē/ō diphthongs surface as ie/uo, and k/g front to c [t͡s] and dz [d͡z] before front vowels. n > ņ is a simplified reflex of Latvian *nj. The old č > s merger has been removed.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: n palatalizes to ɲ before front vowels, a simplified reflex of Latvian ņ from *nj.
k fronts to c [t͡s] before front vowels, a regular Latvian change.
g fronts to dz [d͡z] before front vowels, a regular Latvian change. The demo lexicon has no root g, so the rule is a documented placeholder.

languages.name: Slavic Nahuatl
languages.notes: Proto-Slavic-style daughter of Proto-Balto-Slavic: long ō merges with ā, RUKI š becomes x after [k i], and the first palatalization turns k into č before front vowels. c [t͡s] and č [t͡ʃ] are preserved. The Nahuatl lateral affricate and geminate lateral were already resolved at Proto-Balto-Slavic; the old č > s merger has been removed.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: PBS *ō merges with *ā as long ā, the regular Proto-Slavic merger.
Slavic RUKI: š becomes x after [k i], the Slavic counterpart of the PBS RUKI rule.
First Slavic palatalization: k becomes č before front vowels.

languages.name: Polish Nahuatl
languages.notes: Polish-style daughter of Slavic: vowel length is lost (ā > a, ē > e, ī > i), č and š become the retroflex cz [t͡ʂ] and sz [ʂ], and the parallel l > ł [w] / w > v split is preserved. Slavic *ō had already merged with *ā, so Polish ó [u] is not derived in this demo; no l/ł split is modeled.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: Hard l vocalizes to ł [w]. This rule and w > v are parallel, so inherited w becomes v while the new w from l remains: the Polish ł/w contrast.
Inherited w hardens to v. It stays parallel to l > w, so the new w from l is not fed into this rule.
Polish loses phonemic vowel length: long ā shortens to a.
Polish loses phonemic vowel length: long ē shortens to e.
Polish loses phonemic vowel length: long ī shortens to i.
č becomes the retroflex affricate cz [t͡ʂ].
š becomes the retroflex fricative sz [ʂ].

languages.name: Russian Nahuatl
languages.notes: Russian-style daughter of Slavic: phonemic vowel length is lost, w hardens to v, č becomes the alveolo-palatal [t͡ɕ], and š becomes the retroflex [ʂ]; x is inherited from Slavic. The old prothesis rule and ō > o shortening were removed because the modeled Slavic vowel history leaves them no input, so o remains an inventory vowel but is not derived from the root's o.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: Russian loses phonemic vowel length: long ā shortens to a.
Long ē shortens to e; this is a simplification of the *ě > e outcome in Russian.
Long ī shortens to i.
w hardens to v, the Russian outcome.
č becomes the alveolo-palatal affricate [t͡ɕ], the Russian ч.
š becomes the retroflex fricative [ʂ], the Russian ш.

languages.name: Czech Nahuatl
languages.notes: Czech-style daughter of Slavic: long ē gives í, w hardens to v, and n palatalizes to ň before i/í. Slavic *ō merged with *ā, so Czech ů [uː] and the ú > ou diphthongization are not derived in this demo. The old ō > ů rule has been removed; ř is not modeled.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: Long ē gives Czech í; this is a simplification of the *ě > í outcome.
n palatalizes to ɲ before i/í, a simplification of Czech ň from *nj and front-vowel palatalization.
w hardens to v, the Czech outcome.

languages.name: Proto-Arabic Nahuatl
languages.notes: Proto-Arabic-style branch of the demo: p > f, g > ǧ [d͡ʒ], t͡ʃ > d͡ʒ, kʷ > k, t͡s > s, t͡ɬ > l, and the vowels converge toward the Arabic three-vowel system (o > u, ō > ū, e > i). q, θ, and g remain in the inventory as inherited Arabic phonemes but have no root source in this Nahuatl lexicon; the g > ǧ and q/θ dialect rules are therefore documented placeholders.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: t͡ʃ > d͡ʒ is an adapted substitution that gives the branch an Arabic-shaped ǧ; the more historical source is g > d͡ʒ.
p > f, the one direct Proto-Semitic/Arabic change in the branch.
kʷ simplifies to k, a more natural outcome than the old kʷ > q substitution.
t͡s merges with s, a more natural outcome than the old t͡s > θ substitution.
The lateral affricate merges with l; Arabic has l, and this replaces the old t͡ɬ > ʃ substitution.
Short o converges to u, the main step toward the Arabic three-vowel system.
Long ō converges to ū.
Short e converges to i; Arabic has no short *e.
g > ǧ [d͡ʒ], the historical Arabic source of jīm. The demo lexicon has no root g, so this is a documented placeholder.

languages.name: Peninsular Nahuatl
languages.notes: Peninsular-style daughter of Proto-Arabic: aw and aj monophthongize to ō and ē. The Proto-Arabic vowel convergence is inherited; the old e > ɛ colouring has been removed.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: aw monophthongizes to ō, a Peninsular Arabic change.
aj monophthongizes to ē, the parallel Peninsular change.

languages.name: Gulf Nahuatl
languages.notes: Gulf-style daughter of Peninsular: q fronts to g, ǧ deaffricates to y (a dialectally restricted variant), and k palatalizes to č before front vowels. θ is preserved, as in Gulf Arabic; the vowel system is inherited from Proto-Arabic.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: q fronts to g, a Gulf Arabic feature. The demo lexicon has no root q, so the rule is a documented placeholder.
ǧ deaffricates to y; this is a dialectally restricted Gulf variant, not a categorical law.
k palatalizes to č before front vowels, a Gulf Arabic feature.

languages.name: Bedouin Nahuatl
languages.notes: Najdi/Bedouin-style daughter of Peninsular: q fronts to g, ǧ deaffricates to y (dialectally restricted), and the glottal stop is lost. The glottal loss is simplified because it omits the compensatory lengthening of the historical change.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: ǧ deaffricates to y; this is a dialectally restricted Bedouin/Gulf variant, not a general Najdi law.
q fronts to g, a Najdi/Bedouin feature. The demo lexicon has no root q, so the rule is a documented placeholder.
Simplified Najdi glottal loss: ʔ is deleted without the compensatory lengthening that normally accompanies the historical change.

languages.name: Levantine Nahuatl
languages.notes: Levantine-style daughter of Proto-Arabic: q merges with ʔ, ǧ becomes ž [ʒ], and aw/aj monophthongize to ō/ē. θ is preserved at this node; the Proto-Arabic vowel convergence is inherited.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: q merges with ʔ, a Levantine Arabic change. The demo lexicon has no root q, so the rule is a documented placeholder.
ǧ becomes ž [ʒ], the Levantine reflex.
aw monophthongizes to ō.
aj monophthongizes to ē.

languages.name: Lebanese Nahuatl
languages.notes: Lebanese-style daughter of Levantine: θ stops to t. The old e > ɛ colouring has been removed; the vowel system is inherited from Proto-Arabic/Levantine.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: θ stops to t, the defining Lebanese change.

languages.name: Palestinian Nahuatl
languages.notes: Palestinian-style daughter of Levantine: θ merges with s and k palatalizes to č before front vowels. The inherited Levantine changes and the Proto-Arabic vowel convergence remain.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: θ merges with s in many Palestinian words.
k palatalizes to č before front vowels, the Palestinian k-alternation.

languages.name: Egyptian Nahuatl
languages.notes: Egyptian-style daughter of Proto-Arabic: θ merges with s, and aw/aj monophthongize to ō/ē. q and ǧ are preserved at this node; the Proto-Arabic vowel convergence is inherited.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: θ merges with s in many Egyptian words.
aw monophthongizes to ō.
aj monophthongizes to ē.

languages.name: Cairene Nahuatl
languages.notes: Cairene-style daughter of Egyptian: ǧ stops to g and q merges with ʔ. The old ī > ē colouring has been removed as too broad; long ī is preserved. The vowel system is inherited from Proto-Arabic/Egyptian.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: ǧ stops to g, the Cairene reflex.
q merges with ʔ, the Cairene reflex. The demo lexicon has no root q, so the rule is a documented placeholder.

languages.name: Saidi Nahuatl
languages.notes: Saidi-style daughter of Egyptian: q fronts to g and ǧ becomes the palatal stop ɟ. The inherited Egyptian and Proto-Arabic changes remain.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: q fronts to g, an Upper Egyptian Saidi feature. The demo lexicon has no root q, so the rule is a documented placeholder.
ǧ becomes the palatal stop ɟ, the southern Upper Egyptian reflex.

languages.name: Maghrebi Nahuatl
languages.notes: Maghrebi-style daughter of Proto-Arabic: θ stops to t, ǧ becomes ž [ʒ], and aw/aj monophthongize to ō/ē. q is preserved at this node; the Proto-Arabic vowel convergence is inherited.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: θ stops to t, a Maghrebi change.
ǧ becomes ž [ʒ], the Maghrebi reflex.
aw monophthongizes to ō, a Maghrebi change.
aj monophthongizes to ē, the parallel Maghrebi change.

languages.name: Moroccan Nahuatl
languages.notes: Moroccan-style daughter of Maghrebi: long ē shortens to e. Moroccan Arabic preserves /ʃ/, so the old š > s rule has been removed. The Maghrebi diphthong outcomes and the Proto-Arabic vowel convergence are inherited.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: Long ē shortens to e; a simplification, not a general law.

languages.name: South Arabian Nahuatl
languages.notes: South-Arabian-style daughter of Proto-Arabic: ǧ > d is a constructed lexical/dialectal approximation, word-final hamza is lost, and aw/aj monophthongize to ō/ē. θ, q, and k are preserved at this node; the Proto-Arabic vowel convergence is inherited.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: ǧ > d is a constructed/adapted bridge that approximates a lexical correspondence in some Modern South Arabian varieties; it is not a general law.
Word-final hamza is lost, a plausible South Arabian adaptation.
aw monophthongizes to ō, a South Arabian change.
aj monophthongizes to ē, the parallel change.

languages.name: Mahri Nahuatl
languages.notes: Mahri-style daughter of South Arabian: k spirantizes to x and q yields the ejective ḳ [kʼ]. θ is preserved; the South Arabian monophthongization and the Proto-Arabic vowel convergence are inherited.

phonotactics.notes: Two-consonant onsets and single-consonant codas; penultimate stress.

soundChanges.note: k spirantizes to x, a Mehri change.
q yields the ejective ḳ [kʼ], the Modern South Arabian reflex. The demo lexicon has no root q, so the rule is a documented placeholder.
